subject: Casewise residuals for latent variable models

messages.author: 412732c91cebe3c1
messages.subject: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
parts:
Dear all,


We are trying to model a SEM with observations nested within sites (6 different forests, with in every forest 27 to 43 observations = 202 observations in total). I try to model the interaction between trees, leaf litter quality, soil quality and earthworm components. I hereby hypothesise a positive feedback loop between the different components of our model.


Both multilevel modelling and a lavaan.survey approach do not work for our data as we have to few clusters (=6 forests) (see my previous post “two-level SEM”). Also a multigroup SEM does not work (model can’t converge) as the model has to estimate too much parameters in relation to the number of observations.


Instead, we tried to model our data with a fixed effect SEM including latitude and longitude to correct for spatial autocorrelation. In order to verify whether including latitude and longitude is sufficient to remove the non-independence of our hierarchical data we need to check for spatial autocorrelation in the residuals (fitted response variables-observed).

We extracted the casewise residuals with residuals(fit_modlist, "casewise"), as all response variables in our SEM are latent variables (inferred from open issue #44). The result, however, are very small residual values (e.g. -4.4e-16). It looks like these values are not correct and wonder what we did wrong.

This is our model syntax:

fit_modlist<- '

#latent

Soil =~ pH0_10

worm =~ WormB_McCune

litter =~ litterPCA1

humus =~ humusPCOA1

#regressions

Soil   ~  humus + Lat + Long

worm   ~  Soil + litter + Lat + Long

humus  ~  worm + litter + Lat + Long

'

 

Any advice to solve this would be helpful. Many Thanks!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
parts:
Neitehr of these ideas is an exact answer to your question:
     Your "measurement model" simply equates 4 observed variables with 4 "latent variables"--the latter and identical with the former. The only source of lack of fit is the same as for a path model among observed variables--the missing paths between predictors and dependent variables. If those missing paths are largely consistent with the data, then residuals may be generally small.
     If you use the sem or cfa function to estimate the model, then by default the "latent variables" will be on the same scale as the observed variables. If the observed variables take on small values, then the residuals may also be very small, even if there are substantial discrepancies between model and data.

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
parts:
Hans (?),
Two thoughts spinning off of Ed's comments:

1. As I understand it, the casewise residuals predict the latent variable scores from the observed variables and then predict the observed variables from the latent variable scores using only the measurement model.  Your measurement model must be restricted in ways not shown  in the model code given that you have only one indicator per latent variable.  So, I am not sure what you should expect from casewise residuals in your application.  It is not clear to me that the casewise residuals can help you evaluate the structural part of the model.  Long and Lat are involved only in the structural part of the model.

2. Entering Lat and Long as linear effects assumes a constant linear effect for N/S location and a constant linear effect for E/W location.  That probably does not capture the kinds of patterns you have in mind.  I envision a cluster centered a a particular x,y coordinate and diffusing in every direction from that point.  Even if you include a linear interaction between Lat and Long, this still assumes a monotinic linear effect of, say, Lat on the effect of Long.  So, I wonder if you would not be better off to simply dummy code Forest and treat that as a fixed effect.

Keith
